lesson.title: Skipping the Restart After a Fast Retransmit
lesson.summary: Fast recovery lets TCP cut its congestion window in half rather than collapsing all the way back to slow start after a fast retransmit, since duplicate ACKs show the network is still delivering data.
lesson.body:
Fast retransmit answers the question of when to resend a lost segment, but it leaves open a separate question: what should happen to the congestion window after this kind of loss? The earliest TCP designs, associated with what is now called TCP Tahoe, gave a blunt answer: any loss, however detected, triggers a full return to slow start, resetting cwnd down to its minimum and setting ssthresh to half the window size at the time of loss. That response treats a single lost segment identically to a full-blown network collapse, which is far more conservative than the situation usually warrants.

Fast recovery offers a gentler response for exactly the case fast retransmit handles: loss revealed by duplicate ACKs rather than by a timeout. The reasoning is that duplicate ACKs are only possible if segments sent after the lost one are still reaching the receiver, which means the network is not fully congested or broken, it has just dropped one segment. Collapsing all the way back to a congestion window of one segment would waste the throughput the connection had already earned. Instead, fast recovery cuts the congestion window by half (a multiplicative decrease) and sets ssthresh to that new, halved value, then continues sending at roughly that level rather than crawling back up from scratch through slow start.

The mechanics work like this: when the third duplicate ACK arrives and fast retransmit fires, ssthresh is set to half the current cwnd, and cwnd itself is set to ssthresh plus three segments, the extra three accounting for the three duplicate ACKs already received, each of which represents a segment that has actually left the network and arrived safely at the receiver. As additional duplicate ACKs arrive beyond the third, cwnd is inflated by one more segment each time, since each duplicate ACK is further evidence that another segment has successfully drained from the network. This lets the sender keep transmitting new segments during the recovery period rather than sitting idle. When an ACK finally arrives that acknowledges new data, confirming the retransmitted segment was received, cwnd is deflated back down to ssthresh, and the connection resumes ordinary congestion avoidance from there, rather than restarting slow start from a congestion window of one.

Returning to the earlier trace, suppose cwnd was 20 segments when segment 3 was lost and the three duplicate ACKs triggered fast retransmit. Under fast recovery, ssthresh becomes 10 and cwnd becomes 13 (10 plus 3). If a fourth duplicate ACK arrives before the retransmission is acknowledged, cwnd bumps to 14, and so on. Once the retransmitted segment 3 is acknowledged along with everything after it, cwnd drops to 10 and the connection continues in congestion avoidance, growing by roughly one segment per RTT from there. Compare that to Tahoe's response of dropping to cwnd = 1 and slow-starting all the way back up: fast recovery preserves most of the connection's earned throughput instead of throwing it away. This combination, fast retransmit to detect and repair the loss quickly, fast recovery to avoid an unnecessarily harsh window collapse, is one half of what defines TCP Reno, covered next alongside slow start and congestion avoidance as a complete algorithm.
